scenes.heading: Immunology basics
scenes.sub: Why you rarely catch measles twice
scenes.say: Why do we rarely catch measles twice? Why do vaccines work, and why is HIV so dangerous? It all comes down to how your immune system recognises and remembers invaders.

scenes.heading: Innate vs adaptive
scenes.say: Innate immunity is the security guard: it responds within minutes to anything suspicious, but never learns. Adaptive immunity is the detective with a filing cabinet. It takes days on a new case, targets one specific culprit, and keeps memory cells on file for next time.

scenes.heading: Think of it like this
scenes.everyday: Shops display samples of their goods in the front window
scenes.science: MHC class I displays peptides from inside the cell
scenes.breaks: Cells show only short peptide fragments, and an empty window isn't ignored: NK cells attack cells with too little MHC class I.
scenes.say: Picture every cell as a shop putting samples of what it makes in the window. That's M H C class one. Cytotoxic T cells are guards checking every window. If a virus has taken over, the window shows strange goods, and the guard triggers apoptosis.
scenes.caption: Picture every cell as a shop putting samples of what it makes in the window. That's MHC class I. Cytotoxic T cells are guards checking every window. If a virus has taken over, the window shows strange goods, and the guard triggers apoptosis.

scenes.heading: The rule of 8
points: MHC I × CD8 = 8: cytotoxic T cells
MHC II × CD4 = 8: helper T cells
Helper T cells are the coach
scenes.say: Use the rule of eight. M H C class one times C D eight: cytotoxic T cells. Class two times C D four: helper T cells. Helper T cells are the coach. They switch on B cells and cytotoxic T cells. HIV destroys them, so both arms of adaptive immunity fail.
scenes.caption: Use the rule of 8. MHC class I × CD8: cytotoxic T cells. Class II × CD4: helper T cells. Helper T cells are the coach. They switch on B cells and cytotoxic T cells. HIV destroys them, so both arms of adaptive immunity fail.

scenes.heading: Clonal selection
steps: Memory cells wait for next time
scenes.say: Clonal selection is a shop picking from stock, not tailoring to order. Every lymphocyte's receptor already exists. The antigen selects the matching cell, which copies itself into effector cells to fight now, and memory cells for later.

scenes.heading: What antibodies do: NOAC
scenes.say: Antibodies don't kill pathogens directly. Remember NOAC. Neutralisation blocks viruses and toxins. Opsonisation coats pathogens for phagocytes. Agglutination clumps them together. And complement activation can burst them.

scenes.heading: Primary vs secondary
scenes.question: A rabbit gets antigen X on day 0, then X and Y on day 30. Anti-X peaks at 20 units first, then reaches 450.
lines: First anti-X: slow, peaks at 20 units
Anti-Y: slow, like a first response
Memory is fast, strong and specific
scenes.say: The first anti-X response is slow and peaks at twenty units. After the second dose, anti-X reaches four hundred and fifty: a secondary response from memory cells. But anti-Y looks like a slow first response. Memory is specific, like replaying a game level you've already beaten.
scenes.caption: The first anti-X response is slow and peaks at 20 units. After the second dose, anti-X reaches 450: a secondary response from memory cells. But anti-Y looks like a slow first response. Memory is specific, like replaying a game level you've already beaten.

points: Rule of 8: MHC I–CD8, MHC II–CD4
scenes.say: Quick recap. Innate is fast and general, adaptive is specific with memory. Follow the rule of eight. Antibodies neutralise, opsonise, agglutinate and activate complement. Active immunity lasts, passive immunity, like antivenom, fades. Now try the practice questions!
